title: On the Ground in the Final Days Before Trump’s Midterm Debacle
author: Alec MacGillis
content:
Jacob Hawk leaned over the plastic fencing to get Vivek Ramaswamy’s attention
as the Republican candidate for Ohio governor moved down the line shaking
hands at the Ohio University branch campus in Chillicothe, six days before the
midterm elections. Hawk held onto Ramaswamy’s hand and started trying to tell
him everything he was dealing with, everything he wanted the Republican
candidates gathered there to help him with.

Hawk, 39, told him that he was a self-employed landscaper who was having a
hard time with the high cost of fuel. He told him that he was raising three
young kids from two different moms, mostly on his own. He told him of his
worries for his 9-year-old son, who was autistic and underweight and suffered
from a two-year delay in brain development.

Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, nodded and offered some token reassurance
and moved down the line, toward the arena where he would soon be appearing
with President Donald Trump and Sen. Jon Husted and the rest of the Republican
slate in a state that Trump had won by 11 percentage points two years ago, and
which the party had dominated during the era of Trump. I had been at many
Republican events in the state over that time, including a rally in an
airplane hangar outside Dayton in March 2016, where a giant crowd had roared
as Trump’s jet had rolled into view and where he had declared that he had come
to save Ohio. “Our jobs are being sucked away,” he said then. “It’s
unbelievable what’s happening.”

This event was different. Ten years had passed, and gone was the fierce
bravado of Trump the conquering hero, bristling with retribution and promises.
This rally was populated largely by the same sort of voters who had been
[particularly drawn to Trump all
along](https://www.propublica.org/article/revenge-of-the-forgotten-class),
working-class Midwesterners who had not been engaged in politics before he
came on the scene. But there were fewer of them — the campaign had chosen an
arena that held only 2,000 — and their devotion had been subsumed by
uncertainty. They were still with Trump, but they weren’t sure how to
reconcile their own difficulties with the fact that he was the president
during this trying time.

Take gas prices, which “are beating the hell out of me,” Hawk told me. He was
trying his best not to hold them against Trump and his decision to go to war
against Iran, instead faulting Congress for limiting domestic oil drilling.
“The president has to go find oil in another country because Congress won’t
let him find it in our country,” he said, overlooking the fact that Trump’s
party has controlled both houses of Congress during his second term.

Nearby, Debbie Shock, a 57-year-old mail carrier, blamed the high fuel costs
on “the stock exchange, the markets — they’re the ones that control it.” “We
have oil right here in the U.S.,” she said. “Why are we buying it from other
countries to begin with?”

Shock fit a profile I had gotten to know well in 2016: an Obama-Trump voter.
She was loyal to Trump — “I like the man. Nobody’s perfect, you know what I
mean?” — and told me she would never go back to Democrats now. Why not? I
asked. “They’re covering up the child molestation,” she said. What did she
mean by that? “I’ve heard stories about the sex trafficking. The Clintons are
involved in it, Disney World, you know, all that.”

It would be easy to ridicule such murky talk, yet it was not much less
coherent than what soon emerged on the arena stage, which was streamed on a
large screen for the few hundred of us who were out on the lawn outside the
arena. Trump has never been known for structured oratory, but it is hard to
overstate the extent to which his digressive style has advanced since 2016,
and to convey how surreal it is to experience firsthand, as the reality of
what presidential communication has come to in 2026.

The rally opened with the customary introductory video of late-era Trump, an
explicitly messianic framing: “God said, ‘I need someone who will be strong
and courageous,’” the voice-over intones. “So God made Trump.”

Thus introduced, Trump opened his remarks with a lengthy disquisition on
Husted’s body, which had newly become part of his routine. “I looked at Jon
and studied his physique,” he cooed, after referring to his recent comments on
Husted’s “ass.” “I studied the feet, the legs, the shoulders. I tapped him on
the shoulder, and it was like hitting a piece of steel.”

When a protester inside the arena started shouting something — those of us
outside couldn’t hear what — and was removed, Trump bid him good riddance:
“Now he goes home and his boyfriend gets upset with him.”

There were protesters outside, too, and things were starting to heat up
between them and the supporters. “What are you talking about, ‘boyfriend?’”
shouted one protester, a young man. “He was just talking about Jon Husted’s
ass! That’s not gay??”

A supporter in front of me, a bearded man in his 50s, stewed as he watched the
protesters. “You’re going to see someone dropping like a bad habit,” he
growled, as he started to move toward them, before being held back by the
woman who was with him.

A moment later, Trump had moved on to Jeffrey Epstein, saying that the
Democrats had protected him for years. “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out
of Mar-a-Lago,” he declared. “I was the one who was totally exonerated from
him. But they use it, because that’s what they do. They’re sick, weak people.”

This set off a new round of shouting outside, as cries of “pedophiles!” flew
back and forth.

Suddenly, one Trump supporter near me rushed hard at a protester and knocked
him to the ground, his head landing with such a thud on the blacktop that I
initially thought it might be a suppressed gunshot. Dozens of officers swarmed
to the spot. Cameras flashed.

A few moments later, a couple other protesters, also young men, began railing
against the war against Iran. “We’re going to be the ones sent off to die for
Israel,” one shouted. “‘America First,’ and you want me to die in the Middle
East?”

Trump touched on the war — “they’re getting beaten very badly” — but spent far
more time on his home renovations. “The White House has to be beautiful
outside, it needs that exterior plaster. The bricks were falling, the stone
was broken, the monuments were coming off, the beautiful windows were cracked,
it looked terrible, and I fixed it very inexpensively, and now it’s more
beautiful than ever,” he said. “And President Obama, who doesn’t understand
cleanliness, who doesn’t understand broken cracked stone and sidewalks, who
doesn’t understand that having asphalt going to your main entrance is not the
right thing, we’d like to have granite and marble we’d like to have it look
nice, you don’t use asphalt, you use asphalt for your streets. …”

On the ramble went. To the Haitians in nearby Springfield: “The town went from
no crime to high crime,” but “they’re being moved out.” To a riff on
Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his opponent Amy Acton’s mother calling her a liar,
in apparent reference to Acton’s having accused her stepfather of raping her
when she was 12, as he was subsequently charged with doing. The ad had met
with widespread opprobrium, but Trump defended Ramaswamy. “The mother said
that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar, that she is no good. … How the hell
is that his problem?” To “O Canada, which has been ripping us off for years,”
and Somalia, “which isn’t even a country,” and “transgender mutilization,” and
his plan to rename the Strait of Hormuz for himself.

Finally, Trump ceded the stage to Husted and Ramaswamy. But by then, the lawn
had emptied out as people drifted home, Jacob Hawk among them. A vendor was
shouting out discount prices on his MAGA merchandise. “$10 special on hats!
All the hats are $10! These are normally $25 hats. That’s a good hat for $10.”

* * *

The next day, the full Republican slate of statewide candidates appeared, sans
Trump, at a small pep rally inside a former Delphi auto-parts factory in
Vandalia, outside Dayton. It is an enormous building that employed more than
100 prior to its closing in 2009 and is now being used as a warehouse by a
company that sells air conditioners, employing only 10 or so; Delphi
announcements still remained on the bulletin boards, adding a ghostly feel.

The setting was an unintentional reminder of what Ohio has been through.
Between 2000 and 2025, the state lost 300,000 manufacturing jobs, a
devastation that had [made it highly
susceptible](https://www.propublica.org/article/the-great-republican-crack-up-
dayton-ohio-immigration-donald-trump) to Trump’s message in 2016. But
Republicans have been in charge of the state since 2010, and so it was the
task of the candidates gathered there, with an audience of just a few dozen,
to cast the state as being on an upswing. Complicating this challenge is the
fact that so much of the state’s recent growth has been concentrated in the
Columbus area: countless data centers, defense contractor Anduril, a massive
Intel plant under construction.

The bigger challenge, though, was the nationwide pall that hung over the
event: the reality of stubbornly high inflation and high gas prices, the
latter a direct consequence of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. He had
stood against costly foreign entanglements when he ran in 2016, in opposition
to his party’s recent record, and carried that same banner again in 2024. But
another aspect of his political persona had prevailed: a heedless swagger
that, in this case, had been fanned by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin
Netanyahu and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It had led him into this drawn-
out conflict that has already cost U.S. taxpayers more than $47 billion.

And it had left a long row of Republican candidates standing in this giant
building stacked high with made-in-China air conditioners all but pleading the
small assemblage to save them from the political climate. “You can’t give up,”
Husted said. “This is a Republican state, and the only way Democrats can win
is if Republicans don’t vote.”  

* * *

Five days later, I was in York County, Pennsylvania, which Trump had won by 25
points in 2024, and which was home to one of four Republican-held House
districts targeted by Democrats. I chose to go to a precinct on the outskirts
of York, thinking it would offer a diverse cross-section, in between more
Democratic York proper and more Republican rural areas. But over 90 minutes of
conversations, I didn’t encounter a Republican voter until I was about to call
it a day.

The first person I spoke with, Bill, a 52-year-old state government employee
who asked that I not use his last name for fear of losing his job, had voted
for Trump three times. He hardly considered himself MAGA but was drawn in 2016
to Trump’s “drain the swamp” rhetoric and his disavowal of the war in Iraq. He
voted for him again in 2020 and 2024 because he didn’t think much of Joe Biden
and Kamala Harris.

But on this day, Bill was coming to vote against his Republican
representative, Scott Perry, because he was too “Trump adjacent.” Bill had
finally had enough of Trump, especially when it came to all the revelations of
self-dealing involving his family and cronies. “I will not be falling for him
again,” he told me. “Drain the swamp, no wars. … It was all a lie.”

He said he couldn’t understand how Trump had gone from America First to
seemingly letting the country’s foreign policy be dictated by Israel. He said
that he was voting for the Democrats mainly just for the sake of “gridlock,”
as deliberate blockage. “Someone’s got to stop this,” he said. “It’s getting
out of control.”

Each Democratic voter I spoke with after that was coming with their own
motivation for voting against the Republican slate, like the cast of “Murder
on the Orient Express.”

For Annie (who also asked that I not use her last name), it was for Trump’s
social-welfare cuts, which had cost her and her disabled husband $300 per
month in SNAP benefits and nearly cost them their Medicaid coverage.

For Desiree Edmonds, an elementary school teacher, it was high inflation,
which was translating into anxiety among the working-class children in her
classroom.

For Mark Castillo, a 19-year-old ironworker, it was for the sky-high cost of
diesel.

For Jacqueline Jimenez, a native Puerto Rican who worked as a home-health
aide, it was for the excessive harshness of ICE arrests.

For Shiri Kramer, a warehouse worker, it was for the general meanness
emanating from the administration, which made her think of her grandfather, a
Jewish American who had extended mercy to German POWs during World War II. “My
grandfather would be writhing right now,” she said. “Nothing happening in our
country is OK.”

By night’s end, Republicans had lost this Pennsylvania district by 10 points,
as well as the other three in the state and more than 40 nationwide. They had
lost at least seven Senate seats, even in states where Democrats hadn’t
prevailed in decades — Kansas, Texas, South Carolina. Incredibly, even
Mississippi was on the verge. In Ohio, Republicans lost the race for Senate
and governor — only one of the seven statewide candidates on stage at the
warehouse emerged a victor — as well as two Republican-held House seats, a
stark reversal in a state that had seemed to be trending away from Democrats
for good. In all, Democrats flipped five governorships and up to 12 state
legislative chambers. The Democratic popular-vote margin in congressional
races nationwide was 13 percentage points — nearly double the Republican
margin in their own wave years of 2010 and 1994, and approaching the scale of
the historic Democratic rout in the post-Watergate election of 1974.

The particularly stunning loss of the South Carolina seat brought to mind a
warning issued in May 2016 by Lindsey Graham, whose death this July left the
seat vacant. “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed…….and we will
deserve it,” Graham tweeted in 2016. For years, the Republican Party had
avoided the catastrophic reckoning he warned of — through Trump’s narrow win
in 2016, through [the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the
Capitol](https://projects.propublica.org/parler-capitol-videos/), through
Biden’s fateful insistence on running for reelection at age 81 in 2024. Along
the way, much of the party, including Graham himself, had accommodated itself
to Trump. One way of looking at the 2026 results was that the warning had
finally come true. The reckoning had been delayed by a decade, but it had
gathered more force over time, like a boulder rolling downhill.

There was a hint of such a reckoning in the words that Bill, the three-time
Trump voter, left me with in York. After he returned from voting, he bade me
farewell with a parting regret.

“You see what’s going on,” he said, “and you’re like, ‘What the hell did I
do?’”

The post [On the Ground in the Final Days Before Trump’s Midterm
Debacle](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-movement-rally-voters-
appeal) appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
